q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH?
h: Find the longest chain that includes the carbon bonded to –OH, then number from the end nearer the –OH.
w: The longest chain through the C–OH carbon has 3 carbons, with –OH and a methyl both on C2: 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol). 2-Methyl-1-propanol is a different isomer, (CH3)2CHCH2OH.

q: Which is a secondary (2°) alcohol?
h: Classify by how many carbons are bonded to the carbon that holds the –OH, not by branching elsewhere.
w: In 2-butanol (sec-butyl alcohol) the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is 2°. (CH3)2CHCH2OH is branched but its –OH carbon has only one C neighbor, so it is 1°; (CH3)3COH is 3°.

q: What is the common name of CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Name the two groups on the oxygen alphabetically, then add “ether.”
w: The groups are methyl (CH3–) and propyl (–CH2CH2CH3): methyl propyl ether. Isopropyl would be attached through its middle carbon, –CH(CH3)2.

q: What is the name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH?
h: An –SH group is a thiol; keep the full alkane name and add “-thiol.”
w: Two carbons plus –SH gives ethanethiol. Small thiols smell strongly; ethanethiol is added to natural gas so leaks can be detected.

q: Eugenol, the clove-oil compound dentists use as a mild pain reliever, has an –OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring. Eugenol is classified as a(n)
h: An –OH on an aromatic ring carbon gets its own family name.
w: An –OH bonded directly to a benzene ring makes a phenol. An alcohol has –OH on a carbon that is not part of an aromatic ring.

q: Which statement correctly compares phenol and ethanol in water?
c: Phenol is a weak acid; ethanol is essentially neutral.
Ethanol is a weak acid; phenol is essentially neutral.
Both are strong acids that ionize completely.
Both are weak bases that accept H<sup>+</sup> ions.
h: Which compound can lose H<sup>+</sup> from its –OH and form a stabilized negative ion?
w: Phenol partly ionizes to phenoxide and H3O+, so phenol is a weak acid; ethanol does not ionize appreciably. This mild acidity is part of why phenols act as antiseptics.

q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
h: Which molecule can form hydrogen bonds with its own kind?
w: Only 1-propanol has an O–H that can hydrogen bond between molecules, so CH3CH2CH2OH boils highest (97 °C). The ether has O but no O–H, so it can't H-bond to itself.

q: Which alcohol is the least soluble in water?
h: The –OH is polar, but the hydrocarbon part is nonpolar. Which molecule has the largest nonpolar part?
w: As the carbon chain grows, the nonpolar part takes over; 1-hexanol, with six carbons, is only slightly soluble. Alcohols with 1–3 carbons mix completely with water.

q: 2-Butanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is heated with an acid catalyst. What is the major product?
h: Dehydration removes H and OH to form C=C. Zaitsev's rule picks which H is removed.
w: Zaitsev's rule: the H is removed from the neighboring carbon that has fewer H atoms, giving the more substituted alkene, 2-butene (CH3CH=CHCH3). 1-Butene forms only as the minor product; butanone would be an oxidation product.

q: Rubbing alcohol, 2-propanol, is oxidized with K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. What is the product?
h: A secondary alcohol is oxidized once. What carbonyl compound does that give?
w: Oxidizing a 2° alcohol removes 2 H and gives a ketone: CH3COCH3, propanone (acetone). Aldehydes and carboxylic acids come from 1° alcohols.

q: Which alcohol is NOT oxidized by an oxidizing agent such as K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?
h: Oxidation needs an H atom on the carbon that holds the –OH.
w: In tert-butyl alcohol, 2-methyl-2-propanol, the –OH carbon is bonded to three carbons and has no H, so it is not oxidized. 1° and 2° alcohols are oxidized; 2-methyl-1-propanol is 1° despite its similar name.

q: In the liver, ethanol from alcoholic drinks is first oxidized to
h: Ethanol is a primary alcohol. What does the first oxidation step give?
w: A 1° alcohol is oxidized first to an aldehyde: ethanol → ethanal, which is then oxidized further to acetic acid. Acetaldehyde buildup causes many hangover symptoms.

q: When two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized, as happens when permanent-wave solution reshapes hair keratin, the product contains a(n)
c: sulfide bond (–S–) with loss of S
h: Oxidation removes an H from each –SH. What forms between the two sulfur atoms?
w: 2 R–SH → R–S–S–R + 2 H: a disulfide bond. In hair, disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains are broken and re-formed in new positions.

q: Which compound is a thiol?
h: A thiol is the sulfur version of an alcohol: an –SH group on a carbon.
w: 1-Propanethiol has an –SH group: CH3CH2CH2SH. CH3CH2SCH3 has S between two carbons (a sulfide), CH3SSCH3 is a disulfide, and the –OH compound is an alcohol.

q: Acetic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, and ethanethiol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH, combine by condensation (water is lost). What is the organic product?
h: Treat it like making an ester: –OH from the acid and H from –SH leave as water. Which side keeps the C=O?
w: The C=O stays on the acetic acid side and the S bonds to it, giving a thioester: CH3C(=O)–S–CH2CH3. Acetyl-CoA, the fuel for the citric acid cycle, is a thioester of this type. Putting C=O on the ethyl side reverses the pieces.

q: To which class of alcohol does isobutyl alcohol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH, belong?
h: Go to the carbon holding the –OH and count how many carbons are bonded to it.
w: The –OH carbon is a –CH2– bonded to only one other carbon, so this is a primary (1°) alcohol. The branch is on the next carbon over, so it does not change the classification.

q: Potassium dichromate oxidizes 3-pentanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Which compound forms?
h: Classify the alcohol first: 1° → aldehyde → acid, 2° → ketone, 3° → no reaction.
w: 3-Pentanol is a 2° alcohol (the –OH carbon has two carbons attached and one H), so oxidation turns C–OH into C=O on the same carbon: CH3CH2COCH2CH3 (3-pentanone).

q: With an excess of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, 1-butanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is oxidized as far as it can go. Which compound is the final product?
h: A 1° alcohol is oxidized in two steps. With excess oxidizing agent, does it stop after the first step?
w: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. With excess oxidant the aldehyde (butanal) is oxidized again to CH3CH2CH2COOH, butanoic acid. A ketone can only come from a 2° alcohol.

q: An alcohol with the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives no reaction when treated with K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. Which alcohol is it?
h: To be oxidized, the carbon holding the –OH must still have an H atom to lose.
w: Only a 3° alcohol has no H on the –OH carbon. In (CH3)3COH (tert-butyl alcohol) that carbon carries three CH3 groups, so it is not oxidized. The 2° alcohol would give a ketone and the 1° alcohols an aldehyde/acid.

q: Cyclohexanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, producing cyclohexene and water. This reaction is classified as
h: Compare reactant and product: what small molecule was removed, and was something added or taken away?
w: An –OH and an H from the neighboring carbon leave together as H2O and a C=C forms: an elimination called dehydration. Hydration is the reverse (adding water to an alkene).

q: Which alkene forms in the greatest amount when 2-methyl-2-pentanol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, loses water in hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Remove the OH and an H from a neighboring carbon. When there is a choice, take the H from the neighbor that has fewer H atoms.
w: The –OH carbon (C2) has neighbors CH3 (3 H) and CH2 (2 H). Removing H from the CH2 (fewer H) gives the more substituted alkene, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3 (2-methyl-2-pentene). CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH2CH3 forms too, but only as the minor product.

q: Skunk spray contains the thiol (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH. What is its IUPAC name?
h: An –SH group is a thiol: number the longest chain from the end nearer the –SH, then add the suffix -thiol.
w: The longest chain holding the –SH has 4 carbons; numbering from the –SH end puts SH on C1 and the CH3 on C3: 3-methyl-1-butanethiol. Numbering from the other end (2-methyl-4-...) gives the –SH a higher number, "-butanol" would need –OH, and "pentane" counts the branch into the chain.

q: Ethers are named by listing the two groups on the oxygen. How is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> named?
h: Name the two alkyl groups on the oxygen (watch for a Y-shaped branch), list them alphabetically, then add "ether".
w: One side is –CH2CH3 (ethyl); the other is –CH(CH3)2, a three-carbon Y-shaped group attached through its middle carbon (isopropyl): ethyl isopropyl ether. A propyl group would be the straight –CH2CH2CH3.

q: Number the parent chain so the –OH gets the lowest locant. Which IUPAC name fits CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Number the longest chain from the end that gives the carbon bearing –OH the lowest number.
w: The chain has 5 carbons. Numbering from the right puts –OH on C2 and the methyl on C4: 4-methyl-2-pentanol. Numbering from the left (2-methyl-4-pentanol) gives the –OH a higher number, which is not allowed.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanol, shown, is heated with concentrated H2SO4. What is the major organic product?
h: Dehydration removes H<sub>2</sub>O. Zaitsev's rule: the major alkene has the most carbon groups on the C=C.
w: H2O is lost from the C–OH carbon and a neighboring C–H. Removing the H from the carbon bearing the methyl group gives the more substituted alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene (Zaitsev product). 3-Methylcyclohexene is the minor product; the ketone would require oxidation, not dehydration.

q: 2-Pentanol, shown, is heated with H2SO4. Which is the major alkene formed?
h: The H is removed from the neighboring carbon that has fewer H atoms (Zaitsev's rule), giving the more substituted alkene.
w: The OH carbon (C2) has two neighbors: C1 (CH3) and C3 (CH2). Removing H from C3 puts the C=C between C2 and C3: 2-pentene, the more substituted (major) product. Losing H from C1 gives 1-pentene, the minor product. 2-Pentanone is an oxidation product, and pentane would need H2 added.

q: Isoamyl alcohol (3-methyl-1-butanol), shown, is oxidized with a mild oxidizing agent [O] so that the reaction stops at the first stage. What is the product?
h: A primary alcohol is oxidized first to an aldehyde. Only the carbon bearing the OH changes.
w: The CH2OH carbon loses two H and becomes CHO: 3-methylbutanal. Further oxidation to the carboxylic acid is over-oxidation, which the mild conditions prevent. The ketone oxidizes the wrong carbon, and the alkene is a dehydration product.

q: 1-Butanol, shown, is treated with excess potassium dichromate, K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (a strong oxidizing agent). What is the final organic product?
h: With excess strong oxidizer, a primary alcohol does not stop at the first stage.
w: A 1° alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde, and with excess [O] the aldehyde is oxidized again to butanoic acid. Butanal is only the intermediate. 2-Butanone would require the OH on C2, and 1-butene is a dehydration product.

q: 3-Methyl-2-butanol, shown, is oxidized with [O]. What is the product?
h: Classify the alcohol first. Oxidation turns the C–OH into C=O on the same carbon.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons, so this is a 2° alcohol; it is oxidized to a ketone, 3-methyl-2-butanone. The aldehyde puts the C=O on an end carbon that never had the OH. The alkene comes from dehydration, and the other alcohol just moves the OH.

q: 2-Methyl-2-butanol, shown, is mixed with the oxidizing agent K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> [O]. What happens?
h: Check how many H atoms are on the carbon that holds the OH. Oxidation must remove one of them.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to three carbons, so this is a 3° alcohol. It has no H on that carbon, so it cannot form a C=O: no reaction occurs. The aldehyde, ketone and acid shown would each require moving the oxygen to a different carbon.

q: 1-Propanethiol, shown, gives freshly cut onions part of their odor. When two molecules of it are mildly oxidized [O], what product forms?
h: Oxidation of thiols removes the H from each –SH group and joins the two sulfur atoms.
w: Each –SH loses its H and the two S atoms bond: R–SH + HS–R → R–S–S–R, dipropyl disulfide (the same reaction links cysteines in proteins). The sulfide has lost a sulfur atom, and the peroxide replaces S with O.

q: Which of the alcohols shown is a tertiary (3°) alcohol?
h: Go to the carbon that holds the OH and count how many carbons are bonded to it.
w: In II the C–OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (the methyl and two ring carbons), so II is 3°. I is 1° (the OH carbon has one carbon neighbor, even though the chain is branched), and III and IV are 2°. Branching elsewhere in the molecule does not matter; only the C–OH carbon counts.

q: What is the product of the reaction of cyclohexanol shown?
h: Classify the alcohol first. Oxidation turns C–OH into C=O on the same carbon.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to two ring carbons, so cyclohexanol is a 2° alcohol and oxidizes to the ketone cyclohexanone. Cyclohexene comes from dehydration (H2SO4, heat), not [O]. The aldehyde has an extra carbon, and hexanal would mean the ring broke open.

q: 2-Phenylethanol gives roses their scent. What is the final organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Is the alcohol 1°, 2° or 3°? Excess oxidizing agent keeps going past the first product.
w: The –CH2OH group is a 1° alcohol. Excess [O] oxidizes it to the aldehyde and then on to the carboxylic acid: phenylacetic acid. The aldehyde is only the first product. The ketone puts C=O on the carbon next to the ring, which never held the OH, and styrene is a dehydration product.

q: 1-Hexanol is treated with a mild oxidizing agent, so the reaction stops at the first oxidation product. What is formed in the reaction shown?
h: A 1° alcohol (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH) becomes an aldehyde (–CHO). Keep the same number of carbons.
w: The end carbon loses two H (one from O, one from C) and forms C=O: hexanal. Hexanoic acid is over-oxidation, which needs excess [O]. 2-Hexanone puts the C=O on the wrong carbon, and 1-hexene is a dehydration product.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 4-methyl-2-pentanol shown?
h: The OH is on C2. How many carbons is that carbon bonded to?
w: C2 is bonded to two carbons, so this is a 2° alcohol and gives a ketone at the same carbon: 4-methyl-2-pentanone (methyl isobutyl ketone, a solvent). The aldehyde and the carboxylic acid put C=O on an end carbon, as if the alcohol were 1°. The alkene comes from dehydration, not oxidation.

q: Which compound gives cyclopentanone, shown, when it is oxidized with [O]?
h: A ketone comes from a 2° alcohol oxidized at the same carbon.
w: Cyclopentanol is a 2° alcohol whose OH is on a ring carbon, so [O] turns that C–OH into the ring C=O. Cyclopentylmethanol is a 1° alcohol and gives an aldehyde. 1-Methylcyclopentanol is 3° and does not react. The ring ether has the same formula (C5H10O) as cyclopentanol, but ethers have no O–H and are not oxidized.

q: 1-Methylcyclohexanol is mixed with an oxidizing agent, as shown. What happens?
h: Count the H atoms on the carbon that holds the OH. Oxidation must remove one of them.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and the CH3), so this is a 3° alcohol. With no H on that carbon it cannot form C=O: no reaction. 2-Methylcyclohexanone moves the oxygen to another carbon, 1-methylcyclohexene is a dehydration product (H2SO4, heat), and cyclohexanone would require breaking off the methyl group.

q: All four alcohols shown are isomers of C6H14O. Which one does not react with the oxidizing agent K2Cr2O7?
h: Look at the carbon bonded to the OH. Oxidation needs an H on that carbon.
w: In 3-methyl-3-pentanol the OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (3° alcohol) and carries no H, so it cannot be oxidized. The other choices are 2° alcohols (OH carbon bonded to two carbons, giving ketones) or a 1° alcohol (–CH2OH, giving an aldehyde and then an acid).

q: What is the organic product of the reaction of 3-pentanol shown?
h: Dehydration removes the OH and an H from a neighboring carbon. The C=C forms between those two carbons.
w: The OH is on C3 and both neighbors (C2 and C4) are CH2 groups, so either way the C=C forms between C2 and C3: 2-pentene + H2O. 1-Pentene would need an H removed from C1, which is not next to the OH carbon. 3-Pentanone is an oxidation product, and pentane would need H2.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 2,3-dimethyl-2-butanol shown?
h: The C=C forms toward the neighboring carbon with fewer H atoms (Zaitsev), giving the most substituted alkene.
w: The OH carbon has two kinds of neighbors: CH3 groups (3 H) and a CH (1 H). Removing the H from the CH gives the C=C with four carbon groups: 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, the major product. 2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene (H taken from a CH3) is the minor, less substituted alkene. 3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene has a different carbon skeleton, and the alkane would need H2.

q: Which alkene is the major product of the reaction of 2-methyl-3-pentanol shown?
h: Compare the two carbons next to the OH carbon. The H is removed from the one with fewer H atoms.
w: The OH is on C3. Its neighbors are C2 (CH, 1 H) and C4 (CH2, 2 H). Removing the H from C2 gives the more substituted alkene, 2-methyl-2-pentene (three carbon groups on the C=C). 4-Methyl-2-pentene, from C4, is the minor product. 2-Methyl-1-pentene puts the C=C away from the OH carbon, and the ketone is an oxidation product.

q: Two molecules of 2-propanethiol are oxidized as shown. What is the organic product?
h: Oxidation of thiols removes the H from each –SH and joins the two sulfur atoms.
w: Each –SH loses its H and the two S atoms bond: 2 R–SH + [O] → R–S–S–R + H2O, here diisopropyl disulfide (the same S–S link joins cysteines in proteins). The sulfide has lost a sulfur atom, the peroxide has O in place of S, and dipropyl disulfide attaches S to the end carbon instead of the middle one.

q: Diallyl disulfide, shown, contributes to the odor of garlic. Which thiol forms it when two molecules are oxidized [O]?
h: Split the S–S bond and give each sulfur back its H.
w: Breaking the S–S bond and adding an H to each S gives two molecules of 2-propene-1-thiol (allyl thiol, CH2=CHCH2SH). The alcohol has O instead of S and cannot form an S–S bond. 1-Propanethiol has no C=C, so it gives dipropyl disulfide. Diallyl sulfide has no S–H to oxidize.

q: Name the branched alcohol drawn below, choosing the parent chain correctly.
h: Pick the longest chain that includes the OH carbon, then number from the end that gives the OH the lower number.
w: The longest chain through the OH carbon has five carbons; numbering from the right puts the OH on C3 and the methyl on C2: 2-methyl-3-pentanol. Numbering from the other end gives 4-methyl-3-pentanol (same OH locant, but the substituent gets the higher number, so it is wrong). 3-Ethyl-2-butanol uses a shorter chain, and "hexanol" counts six carbons that are not there.

q: Thiols give skunk spray and natural gas their warning odors. Which of these drawings is a thiol?
h: A thiol is the sulfur analog of an alcohol: –SH on a carbon.
w: Only the first structure has an –SH group (1-butanethiol, a skunk-like odorant). The –OH compound is an alcohol; the C–S–C compound is a sulfide (thioether); the S–S compound is a disulfide, the product of oxidizing two thiols.

q: Linalool, shown, gives lavender and coriander their scent. How is the alcohol group at carbon a classified?
c: tertiary (3°): the OH carbon is bonded to three other carbons
secondary (2°): the OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons
primary (1°): the OH carbon is bonded to one other carbon
it is a phenol, because the molecule contains double bonds
h: Go to the carbon that holds the OH and count the C–C bonds it makes; ignore the rest of the molecule.
w: Carbon a is bonded to a methyl group, a vinyl (CH=CH2) group and the long chain: three carbons, so it is a 3° alcohol (and would not be oxidized). The double bonds elsewhere do not change the classification, and a phenol needs the OH on a benzene ring, which linalool does not have.

q: Methanethiol condenses with propanoic acid when the two are heated, losing water. Which drawing is the sulfur-containing product?
h: Treat the thiol like an alcohol: the acid loses –OH, the thiol loses its H, and C(=O)–S forms. Sulfur stays in the product.
w: Condensation of a carboxylic acid with a thiol gives a thioester, CH3CH2C(=O)–S–CH3: the C=O side comes from the acid and the S from the thiol. The ester (C(=O)–O–CH3) is the product with an alcohol, not a thiol. The thioester with the groups swapped would have to come from acetic acid and ethanethiol. A sulfide (C–S–C with no C=O) requires losing the carbonyl, which does not happen.

q: A thioester is formed when a thiol condenses with a carboxylic acid. How does a thioester differ structurally from an ordinary ester?
c: A sulfur atom replaces the single-bonded oxygen between the C=O carbon and the alkyl group.
A sulfur atom replaces the double-bonded oxygen of the C=O group, giving a C=S double bond.
A sulfur atom replaces the carbonyl carbon itself, so the group becomes O=S bonded to oxygen.
An –SH group is added to the carbonyl carbon alongside the –OR group, with no atoms removed.
h: Where does the sulfur of the thiol end up? The thiol loses only its H.
w: The thiol R–SH plays the role of the alcohol R–OH, so its S ends up where the ester's single-bonded O would be: R–C(=O)–S–R′. The C=O group is unchanged (it comes from the acid). Acetyl-CoA, the key thioester of metabolism, has exactly this C(=O)–S linkage.
